```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
summary <- readr::read_csv("results/data_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
approval <- readr::read_csv("results/approval_estimates.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
election <- readr::read_csv("results/election_estimates.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
runtime <- jsonlite::read_json("results/approval_runtime.json")
approval_holdout <- readr::read_csv("results/approval_holdout.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
weighted_approval <- readr::read_csv("results/approval_sensitivity.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(house == "Rasmussen", specification == "sample_size")
rasmussen_approval <- readr::read_csv("results/polls.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(dataset == "approval", house == "Rasmussen", is.na(exclusion))
format_effect <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%+.1f pp (95%% credible interval %+.1f to %+.1f)", x$estimate, x$lower, x$upper)
}
house_table <- function(x) {
  x |>
    dplyr::filter(reference) |>
    dplyr::arrange(house) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      House = house, `Effect (pp)` = round(estimate, 1),
      `95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", lower, upper),
      Polls = n_polls, Support = support
    ) |>
    knitr::kable()
}
```

# The House Always Wins: House Effects in Polling

How much do polling organizations differ when measuring the same political
outcome at comparable times and places? This project estimates **relative house
effects** from historical Bush approval polls and 2008 presidential election
polls. The estimates describe these datasets and periods, not the current
performance of polling organizations.

Rasmussen's estimated Bush-approval house effect is
**`r format_effect(dplyr::filter(approval, house == "Rasmussen"))`**.
Its estimated effect on the McCain-minus-Obama margin is
**`r format_effect(dplyr::filter(election, house == "Rasmussen"))`**.
The reference in each analysis is the equal-weight average of houses with at
least ten usable polls in at least three calendar months. Positive values mean
higher Bush approval or a more Republican election margin than that reference.

These are differences from other pollsters, not errors against known public
opinion. Polling consensus can itself be wrong. A house effect includes the
organization's population screens and other practices; it does not identify
their individual contributions or establish intentional bias.

Results can depend on sample availability and modeling choices. Rasmussen's
sample-size-weighted approval estimate is
**`r format_effect(weighted_approval)`**, retaining only
`r sum(!is.na(rasmussen_approval$sample_size))` of its
`r nrow(rasmussen_approval)` usable polls. This sensitivity changes both the
sample and the error model, so it cannot isolate the effect of weighting.

## Bush approval

The analysis uses `r summary$usable_polls[summary$dataset == "approval"]` polls,
covering `r summary$first_date[summary$dataset == "approval"]` through
`r summary$last_date[summary$dataset == "approval"]`.

![Bush approval house effects](figs/approval_houses.png)

```{r approval-table, results='asis'}
house_table(approval)
```

## 2008 presidential election

The analysis uses `r summary$usable_polls[summary$dataset == "election"]` polls,
covering `r summary$first_date[summary$dataset == "election"]` through
`r summary$last_date[summary$dataset == "election"]`. National polls and state
polls have separate geographic levels and trends. The outcome is McCain support
minus Obama support, without renormalizing away other candidates or undecided
respondents. A two-point effect on this margin is not a two-point effect on one
candidate's vote share.

![Election house effects](figs/election_houses.png)

```{r election-table, results='asis'}
house_table(election)
```

The tables show houses meeting the reference coverage rule, without filtering
on statistical significance. The complete [approval estimates](results/approval_estimates.csv)
and [election estimates](results/election_estimates.csv) include sparse houses,
their intervals, coverage dates, and overlap measures. In the CSVs, `estimate`
and `sd` are the posterior mean and standard deviation; `lower` and `upper`
are the 95% interval bounds. Sparse estimates depend
more heavily on partial pooling. Intervals are marginal credible intervals,
not simultaneous guarantees for all houses or a ranking of accuracy.

## Model and checks

| Model | Role | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| House and geography-month fixed effects | Descriptive benchmark | Transparent within-cell comparisons; sparse or disconnected houses are poorly identified |
| Bayesian Student-t model | Published estimates | Partial pooling and joint uncertainty; depends on time, geography, and dependence assumptions |
| Gaussian model with approximate sampling variances | Sensitivity analysis | Uses reported sample sizes; excludes missing sizes and assumes unobserved design effects away |

Separate Bayesian Student-t models combine partially pooled house intercepts,
smooth time trends, and correlated errors within each house and fortnight.
Approval includes an explicit September 11, 2001 break so the trend does not
spread the abrupt change into earlier polls. Election models also
include geography intercepts and partially pooled cubic spline deviations by
geography. The model uses reported percentage-point outcomes, not invented
respondent-level counts. Missing sample sizes therefore do not remove polls
from the primary analysis.

House effects are constant within each historical dataset. Differences in
question wording, survey mode, sponsorship, and populations may remain inside
these estimates. Time trends approximate opinion over fieldwork using its
midpoint. Within-fortnight correlation addresses some dependence but cannot recover
unobserved respondent overlap. Limited comparison support is measured using
shared geography-month cells and explicitly flagged.

The [model report](docs/audit.md) documents data handling,
fixed-effects benchmarks, sample-size and screen adjustments, alternate time
trends, four-week dependence blocks, nonoverlapping fieldwork samples, influential-house exclusions,
posterior predictive checks, and simulated-data recovery. National-only and
McCain-support analyses are also provided. These are sensitivity analyses of
historical relative effects, not election forecasts.

Forward prediction is poor for approval: training through
`r approval_holdout$cutoff` gives `r round(approval_holdout$rmse, 1)`-point RMSE
on the later polls, with `r round(100 * approval_holdout$predictive_coverage_95, 1)`%
coverage from nominal 95% predictive intervals. These are retrospective
adjustment models; the approval model should not be used to forecast opinion.

## Reproduce

Use R 4.6 or newer, a working C++ toolchain, Make, and Pandoc. The recorded run uses
R `r runtime$r_version`, `brms` `r runtime$packages$brms`, and CmdStan
`r runtime$cmdstan`. Dependency versions are recorded in `renv.lock`.

```sh
make setup
make all
```

`make setup` restores R packages into `.r-library` and installs CmdStan 2.40.0
into the ignored project cache. An explicit `CMDSTAN` environment variable can
select another installation. Full Bayesian fits and sensitivity runs can take
many hours; cached fits are reused when their data and statistical model
match. To change sampling controls, iteration counts, or software versions for an existing fit,
remove its named `.rds` file from `cache/` before refitting.

```sh
make test
make lint
make ci-docker
make render
```

`make ci-docker` runs tests, lint, and published-artifact checks in the standard
`rocker/verse:4.6.0` image. The GitHub workflow additionally fits a simulated
Bayesian model. `make render` rebuilds this README and the audit report from
saved results; analytical numbers are not maintained by hand. Fits are cached
during estimation and can be deleted after the reports and checks finish.
CSV estimates, generated Stan programs, diagnostics, and session information
are committed in `results/`.

## Data

These data were collected in 2007–2008 to examine house effects and differences
in polling practices. The original sources included PollingReport.com and
Pollster.com. This repository retains the original
[Bush approval data](data/bushfav_merged.csv) and
[election data](data/collapsed%20polls_pollster.csv).

The cleaned [poll-level data](results/polls.csv) retain source rows and flag
observations excluded from estimation.
The election CSV has two source columns named `n`; the importer preserves both
under distinct names and checks their agreement. Unverified dates are excluded
rather than silently repaired. The audit explains what can and cannot be
verified from these historical files.

The original descriptive figures remain in `figs/approve_rasmussen.png` and
`figs/mccain_rasmussen.png`; they are not the adjusted house-effect estimates.
